concept_card.subtopic: Oscillations: mean position, displacement and amplitude
concept_card.learning_objective: Students will be able to locate the mean position of an oscillating body, measure displacement from it, find the amplitude as half the distance between the extreme positions, and tell periodic, oscillatory and simple harmonic motion apart.
concept_card.statement: In an oscillation, displacement is measured from the mean (equilibrium) position, and the amplitude is the maximum displacement: the distance from the mean position to either extreme, which is half the extreme-to-extreme distance.
concept_card.simple: An oscillating body goes back and forth around the point where it would rest, called the mean position. How far it is from that point right now is its displacement. The farthest it ever gets from that point is the amplitude. So the amplitude is only half the gap between the two ends.
concept_card.formal: Periodic motion repeats after equal intervals of time. Oscillatory motion is periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position, where the net force on the body is zero. Simple harmonic motion is the special oscillation in which the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position, F = -kx. Displacement x is measured from the mean position and varies between +A and -A. The extreme positions are at x = ±A, so they are 2A apart.

equations.meaning: Displacement from the mean position at time t in SHM
Distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude
equations.assumptions: symmetric oscillation about the mean position, no damping

equations.meaning: Restoring force in SHM is proportional to displacement and points towards the mean position
equations.assumptions: ideal SHM; small displacements for a pendulum

concept_card.analogy: A park swing: the lowest point, where it would hang at rest, is the mean position. The amplitude is how far the seat gets from that lowest point on one side, not the full distance from the front end to the back end.
steps: Locate the mean position: where the body would rest with zero net force, midway between the extremes
Measure displacement from the mean position, with a sign showing the side
Mark the extremes, where the displacement is largest: x = +A and x = -A
Take the amplitude as half the distance between the two extremes
Call the motion SHM only if the restoring force is proportional to -x
concept_card.worked_example: A block oscillates between extremes 0.20 m apart. A = 0.20 m / 2 = 0.10 m. When it is 0.04 m from one extreme, its displacement from the mean is 0.10 - 0.04 = 0.06 m, on that extreme's side. If it starts at that extreme at t = 0, x = 0.10 cos(ωt) m, so φ = 0.
alternatives: Picture a number line with zero at the mean position: the body runs between -A and +A. It travels 2A from one end to the other, but its amplitude is just A.
Every SHM is periodic, but not every periodic motion is SHM: Earth's orbit and a bouncing ball repeat, yet neither has a restoring force F = -kx about a mean position.
concept_card.source: Seeded draft written for LearnLoop AI; requires academic review against the Maharashtra State Board HSC Physics textbook. No textbook citation is claimed.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: Amplitude is the whole distance the block moves, from one end to the other.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: The two ends are easiest to see, so measuring end to end feels natural.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Amplitude is the maximum displacement, measured from the mean position. The extremes are at +A and -A, so they are 2A apart.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Amplitude is the distance from the mean position to either extreme, half the end-to-end distance.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Pause the block at the right extreme: x reads +A, not 2A. At the left extreme x reads -A.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: If it repeats at equal time intervals, it is SHM.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: SHM is the first repeating motion we study, so periodic and SHM seem to mean the same.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Periodic only means it repeats. SHM also needs a restoring force F = -kx. A bouncing ball repeats but has no such force.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Every SHM is periodic, but a periodic motion is SHM only if its acceleration is proportional to -x.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Watch the a-x graph: a straight line through the origin, a opposite to x. That, not repetition, marks SHM.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: Displacement means how far it has gone from where I released it.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: In straight-line motion we measure displacement from the starting point.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: In an oscillation the reference is the mean position, where net force is zero. The release point is just one extreme and changes with each release.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Displacement is measured from the mean position, with sign, ranging from -A to +A.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Release from the right extreme: x reads +A at release and 0 at the centre. Release from the left: zero stays at the centre.

contrast_probes.probe: What would you need to check before saying a repeating motion is 'SHM with an amplitude of 5 cm'?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: That it is SHM, and that its two ends are 5 cm apart.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Only that it repeats at equal intervals, and that it goes 5 cm out from the middle.

contrast_probes.probe: A pendulum released from one extreme swings between extremes 8 cm apart; what is its displacement when it is exactly at the middle?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Zero, it is at the mean position, though the amplitude is the full 8 cm.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: 4 cm, because it has moved halfway from where it was released.

contrast_probes.probe: For a ball bouncing on the floor, is the motion SHM, and where is its displacement zero?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It repeats, so it is SHM, with zero displacement at the middle of its bounce height.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Its displacement is zero at the floor, because that is where each bounce starts.

contrast_probes.probe: A swing's two extreme points are 2 m apart; how far is each extreme from the lowest point, and what is the amplitude?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Each extreme is 1 m from the bottom, but the amplitude is 2 m because that is the full swing.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Each extreme is 1 m from the lowest point, so the amplitude is 1 m.

contrast_probes.probe: Earth goes round the Sun once every year; is that motion SHM?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, it repeats every year, so it is SHM.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, it is periodic, but it is not to-and-fro about a mean position with a force proportional to -x.

contrast_probes.probe: A block released 5 cm to the right of the mean position is now 2 cm to the right of it; what is its displacement?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: 3 cm, because it has moved 3 cm from where it was released.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: +2 cm, measured from the mean position.

doubts.a: No. Amplitude is the maximum distance from the mean position, so it is always positive. Displacement can be negative, for example x = -A at the other extreme; the sign only shows which side of the mean the body is on.

doubts.q: Why do we measure displacement from the mean position and not from where we release the body?
doubts.a: The mean position is where the net force is zero, and the motion is symmetric about it, so it stays the same however you start the motion. The release point is just one extreme and can change from trial to trial.

No. Oscillatory only means to-and-fro motion about a mean position. It is SHM only when the restoring force is proportional to displacement, F = -kx. A pendulum swinging through large angles oscillates but is not exactly SHM.

doubts.q: How much distance does the body cover in one complete oscillation?
doubts.a: In one oscillation it goes from the mean to one extreme, back through the mean to the other extreme, and back to the mean, covering 4A. Its displacement after one full oscillation is zero, since it returns to the same point.
